chunks: Al-Saduq's Book of Unity and his Amali: My father, from Sa'd, from al-Yaqtini, who said:

Abu al-Hasan the Third (peace be upon him) wrote to one of his Shia in Baghdad: In the Name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. May Allah protect us and you from the trial. If He does, then count it a great blessing, and if He does not, then it is perdition. We consider argumentation about the Qur'an to be an innovation, in which both the questioner and the respondent have partaken. So the questioner has engaged in what is not for him, and the respondent has borne what is not on him. There is no creator except Allah, and what is other than Him is created. The Qur'an is the Speech of Allah. Do not make for it a name from yourself, so you will be among the astray. May Allah make us and you of those who 'fear their Lord without seeing Him and are of the Hour apprehensive.'

key_terms.يَخْشَوْنَ رَبَّهُمْ بِالْغَيْب: Those who fear their Lord in the unseen

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia view on debating the creation of the Qur'an according to Imam al-Hadi?
ai.summary: In this letter, Imam al-Hadi (peace be upon him) cautions his Baghdad followers against the theological innovation (bid'ah) of debating the Qur'an's nature, emphasizing that while the Qur'an is the uncreated Speech of Allah, it is distinct from the Divine Essence itself. This position reflects the early Shia stance against both the Mu'tazila's 'created Qur'an' and the Hanbalis' 'uncreated Qur'an' extremes, advocating for a balanced understanding that avoids attributing human names to the Divine Speech. The narration concludes by linking this theological humility to the Quranic ideal of those who fear their Lord in the unseen, reinforcing the spiritual consequence of correct belief.
